title: STIT logic
summary:
STIT logic (seeing to it that) is a formal logical framework for reasoning about agency and action. The term "stit" is an acronym based on "sees to it that." The idea is to add, to an ordinary classical propositional language, a new propositional operator, interpreting stit_i(phi) as "agent i sees to it that phi." STIT theory grew out of the philosophical tradition of modal logic and was created by Nuel Belnap and his many collaborators.

One important difference between STIT logic and dynamic logic is that actions are not directly studied in stit theory: the ontology does not usually recognize a category of actions or events, whereas dynamic logic does. A stit frame has four components: a set T, the nodes of which are called moments; an irreflexive tree ordering of T; a set of agents; and a choice function C. A maximal branch through the tree is called a history.

A number of the initial papers defining the stit tradition are collected in the volume Belnap (2001), titled Facing the Future: Agents and Choices in Our Indeterminist World. One important later work is John F. Horty's book Agency and Deontic Logic (2001). The logic of stit was axiomatized by Ming Xu in 1998.

Broersen, partially jointly with Herzig and Troquard, has shown several connections such as embeddings of Coalition Logic and ATL in forms of stit logic and extensions of stit and ATL to cater for reasoning about interesting properties of multi-agent systems. STIT logic has been extended in various directions, including temporal STIT logic for reasoning about multi-agency with applications for reasoning about norms, knowledge, autonomy, and other multi-agent concepts. Extensions also include deontic STIT logic with beliefs and expected utility, and a logic of responsibility extending stit theory with epistemic, doxastic, deontic, and intentional modalities.
